To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) DLC are generated by repetitive allostimulation of spleen cells; (2) DLC are similar to DC, including morphology and surface marker expression; (3) DLC have potent antigen‐presenting function and are differentially regulated by GM‐CSF and IL‐4.
long‐term allostimulation in mixed leucocyte reactions can induce a population of dendritc cell‐like cells with potent antigen‐presenting function.
a population of APC with dendritic cell‐ like characteristics can be induced from spleen cells in long‐ term mixed leucocyte reactions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of APC proliferation, differentiation and regulation of their functions.
the generation, characterization, regulation and function of APC in vivo and in vitro.

the mechanisms underlying the proliferation of APC precursors in response to antigen stimulation, the differentiation of APC precursors into mature APC and the functional role of cytokines in APC development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
these cells are not DC.
these cells are a new population of DLC which can be induced in vitro from spleen cells by repetitive allostimulation.
DLC generated in LT‐MLC are a population of DC‐like cells which are capable of proliferating and persisting in culture, and which are potent APC.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DLC are a unique population of APC that are capable of self‐renewal and can be generated by repetitive alloantigen stimulation in LT‐MLC.

we have successfully established a new model system for studying the proliferation and differentiation pathways of APC, which may be applicable to other professional APC, such as DC and Langerhans cells.
the generation of DLC from spleen cells by repetitive allostimulation may provide a useful model system for studying the differentiation of APC from haemopoietic progenitors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the DLC are a good model to study the proliferation, differentiation and functional regulation of DC in vivo.
DLC can be induced from unfractionated splenocytes and that the proliferation and differentiation is regulated by cytokines.
DC can be generated in long‐term culture, which can be used as an in vitro model to study the biology of DC and the mechanism of antigen presentation.
